segments.title: Birth name, the name Paquito, and growing up near the Tropicana
segments.summary: He gives his birth name, explains Paquito as a diminutive of Francisco, and says he was born June 4, 1948 in Marianao, Havana, ten blocks from the Tropicana, where his father sold instruments.

segments.title: Parents, siblings and the extended Cuban family
segments.summary: Names, origins and ages of his parents, his brother and sister, and the large family on his mother's side.

segments.title: Close family life and his parents' schooling
segments.summary: The family stayed close; his mother studied nursing but stopped when she married, and his father took up the saxophone as a teen and grew up surrounded by Tropicana musicians.

segments.title: How his father became a classical saxophonist
segments.summary: His father left a print shop apprenticeship for music, studied with a private teacher, graduated from a conservatory and imported the French saxophone school, founding a saxophone ensemble in 1946.

segments.title: His father's instrument business and visiting Havana musicians
segments.summary: His father sold saxophones, clarinets and music from a small office, where Cachao, Chocolate Armenteros and Mario Bauza came by; his mother was a seamstress.

segments.title: All kinds of music at home: Mozart, Webern, Goodman, Machito
segments.summary: His father believed in only good music and bad music, so Paquito heard classical, swing and Cuban music side by side; his father gave up a solo career to nurture his son.

segments.title: Cachao, Chocolate and his father's musician friends
segments.summary: The musicians met at a standing-room bar near his father's office; as a child he inherited their friendship and wanted to be as elegant as Chocolate Armenteros.

segments.title: First soprano saxophone at five and first public performance
segments.summary: His father imported a soprano saxophone in 1953, taught him, and nine months later presented him at a school show with a swing piece among three tunes.

segments.title: Learning to read music first; his strict father
segments.summary: His father made him read and chant music before touching the sax, which Paquito defends against jazz players who skip reading; he calls his father a nice dictator and a fellow practical joker.

segments.title: No choice: his father's constant practicing and how lessons began
segments.summary: His father practiced all the time and taught him by example, so becoming a musician was a natural development.

segments.title: Havana Conservatory and leaving school for music
segments.summary: He entered the conservatory around 1959-60 for theory and harmony, regrets never studying abroad, and persuaded his father to let him leave school for full-time music study.

segments.title: Boy wonder of the saxophone on TV and with orchestras
segments.summary: As a child prodigy he did TV shows from about age six, recitals and played transcribed Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman solos with orchestras.

segments.title: Clarinet: his father teaches, then Enrique Pablo
segments.summary: His father taught him clarinet without playing it, until he took Paquito to Enrique Pablo, first clarinet of the Havana Philharmonic, who shaped his technique.

segments.title: His brother and sister did not become musicians
segments.summary: His brother played piano and sax but became a painter-minded person; only he and his father were professional musicians.

segments.title: His father after the revolution: army, theater, lost business
segments.summary: His father retired from the army, taught older people and played in a theater; when Castro took power his instrument business ended and the Paris study plan collapsed.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Drafted into the army and discharged early
segments.summary: He left high school at 15-16 for the army, served about two and a half years, and was released early thanks to a commander who liked to compose.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Teatro Musical de La Habana orchestra with Alfonso Arau
segments.summary: From age 13 to 15 he played in the orchestra of a theater company founded by Alfonso Arau while still at the conservatory.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Army band and finishing the conservatory in uniform
segments.summary: In the army concert band with strong young players, he continued clarinet studies and gave his graduation recital dressed as a soldier.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Founding the Orquesta Cubana de Musica Moderna
segments.summary: The government formed a big band in 1967 to play formerly banned jazz and American music for visiting Black activists; Paquito, Chucho Valdes and Leo Brouwer were first called under Armando Romeu.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Race among Cuban musicians and in the army
segments.summary: He says race was not a factor among musicians, since the best were Black, though in the army and party most officers and conductors were white.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Political control of music and the exit-visa wait
segments.summary: After the revolution jazz was treated as the enemy, the state controlled what, when and with whom you played, and leaving required waiting up to twenty years.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Secret jazz sessions and the Monday jazz club
segments.summary: Jazz was never a living, only a hobby: house sessions on borrowed pianos and a club with jazz Mondays under the eye of the political police.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: His father introduces him to bebop with Charlie Parker LPs
segments.summary: His father played a Parker LP, Paquito did not like it, and his father insisted they learn it, bringing bebop books and records until they both loved it.

segments.chapter: Army, politics and jazz in Cuba
segments.title: Growing to like bebop and hearing the Miles Davis quintet on Voice of America
segments.summary: He took to bebop quickly, enjoyed a Kenton baritone player, then listened secretly to Willis Conover and found the new Miles Davis quintet puzzling.

segments.title: Repertoire and purpose of the officially formed big band
segments.summary: The orchestra played music banned months earlier, such as Route 66 and Mancini, on imported instruments; Paquito believes it was formed to counter the image that the revolution blocked jazz, and it got him out of the army.

segments.title: Armando Romeu, instrumentation and the Kenton charts
segments.summary: Led by Romeu, the band had five saxes, four trombones, five trumpets, two drummers and percussion, and played a lot of Stan Kenton arrangements transcribed in hours.

segments.title: Government dictates the orchestra; the varied tastes of its members
segments.summary: Everything had a political aim, yet the band held musicians with many tastes from Chucho's Oscar Peterson to bossa nova and commercial Mancini hits.

segments.title: The orchestra's goal accomplished and Irakere's origin
segments.summary: Its splendor lasted one or two years; once it removed the anti-jazz accusation against the government, it faded, and Irakere followed.

segments.title: Becoming director of the orchestra in 1970
segments.summary: When Romeu left and members drifted away, Paquito took over for a year and refused to back pop singers.

segments.title: Jazz repertoire and pointless gigs as director
segments.summary: He programmed jazz, his own pieces and Chucho and Romeu arrangements, but jazz was again imperial music, and the band played mostly useless pub and theater gigs.

segments.title: The minister of culture sends him home to rest
segments.summary: After a year as conductor he got a call telling him to rest for his own safety, and was paid a salary for two years of doing nothing, a paid musical exile.

segments.title: Conducting the Tropicana orchestra for meals; the depression
segments.summary: He played for free and conducted the Tropicana show orchestra for food for a month, while the enforced idleness was meant to depress and warn him.

segments.title: His first brief marriage and meeting his second wife
segments.summary: He married Maria, a harpist, in 1968 for nine months because of his womanizing, then met his second wife at a university concert; that marriage lasted about ten years.

segments.title: Free playing with Emiliano Salvador before Irakere
segments.summary: During the idle period he wrote charts, played unpaid with pianist Emiliano Salvador and Carlos del Puerto and with the film-industry sound experimentation group, with no steady gig until Irakere.

segments.title: Chucho Valdes recruits him for Irakere
segments.summary: Chucho invited him to a park, explained the plan for an internationally known group called Irakere, and said never to use the word jazz.

segments.title: Irakere's original lineup and its fusion of rhythms
segments.summary: The first lineup and how Oscarito Valdes's percussion and singing, Chucho's Peterson-influenced piano, and Paquito's Mozart-based piece created a new sound.

segments.title: Early travel restrictions and his assigned minder Enrique Pla
segments.summary: He was kept home at first; early tours went to Bulgaria, Hungary, then Jamaica and Finland, where drummer Enrique Pla, a party member, was assigned to guard him but admitted it.

segments.title: How Irakere won permission to tour: Oscarito Valdes
segments.summary: He credits Oscarito Valdes, who had links to government and political police, with organizing the group so that it could travel.

segments.title: Bacalao con Pan and Irakere's early Egrem hits
segments.summary: The band's first piece became an immediate Cuban hit and was followed by more Egrem releases; the group was very popular on the island.

segments.title: 1977: Dizzy Gillespie's note and the call to Havana Libre
segments.summary: Dizzy Gillespie, Stan Getz and Earl Hines arrived on a cruise ship; Dizzy left a note at Paquito's house after Arturo Sandoval brought him there, and Paquito was summoned to the hotel.

segments.title: The 1977 jam session with Getz and talk with Ray Mantilla
segments.summary: Irakere and Los Papines jammed with Stan Getz, Ray Mantilla and Mickey Roker; backstage Paquito first heard Spanglish.

segments.title: CBS flies to Havana; the government suspected jazz
segments.summary: Dizzy and Getz alerted Bruce Lundvall, who flew to Havana; until then officials had blocked the band as suspected jazz musicians, which Chucho publicly denied.

segments.title: Havana Jam 1978 and traveling to the US and Montreux
segments.summary: After American approval the band traveled more; CBS organized Havana Jam in 1978, and the band went on to New York and Switzerland.

segments.title: The Fania All Stars and Weather Report at Havana Jam
segments.summary: Cubans were unimpressed by the Fania All Stars but startled by Weather Report and the Trio of Doom.

segments.title: Impressions of Woody Shaw, Stan Getz and Hubert Laws
segments.summary: He admired Woody Shaw's trumpet sound and Stan Getz's timbre and swing, and felt their praise of Irakere was the best reward.

segments.title: Irakere's first CBS records and a Grammy
segments.summary: After the live recording they recorded Irakere, which won a Grammy, then Irakere II, when Lundvall proposed a solo LP, and CBS gave the group world exposure.

segments.title: Cuban officials, dual repertoire and defining jazz
segments.summary: Irakere kept separate concert and dance repertoires, with the jazz spirit in both; when Americans labelled it jazz, officials said it was too late.

segments.title: First trip to New York, Switzerland and the 1979 Stills tour
segments.summary: Irakere flew to New York with the Americans, played Carnegie Hall in 1978, toured Switzerland, and returned in 1979 for a tour with Stephen Stills; Bebo Valdes happened to be visiting.

segments.title: Irakere at Carnegie Hall in 1978 on a piano night
segments.summary: Unannounced, Irakere followed Mary Lou Williams, McCoy Tyner and Bill Evans; the Cuban minder tried to stop Stan Getz sitting in, and the audience loved it.

segments.title: Bebo Valdes and Chucho meet after twenty years
segments.summary: Bebo came to New York and wanted to see his son; Chucho was afraid of contact with exiles, and Paquito carried messages for their brief meeting.

segments.title: His parents emigrate to New York
segments.summary: His mother left in 1968 and his father in 1970; his father never played again, while his mother worked in the garment district.

segments.title: Touring with Stephen Stills in 1979
segments.summary: Irakere opened 22 East Coast concerts for Stephen Stills; the rock audience did not respond, and Paquito felt it did not help them.

segments.title: First impressions of touring America
segments.summary: Touring American universities and arenas felt like a toy store compared with life in a Communist country.

segments.title: Why he did not defect in 1979 and what changed in 1980
segments.summary: With a wife and young son held as hostages in effect, he stayed; the 1980 Peruvian Embassy crisis made him decide to leave on the next trip.

segments.title: Deciding to defect on the May 1980 European tour
segments.summary: Broken instruments and the Mariel and embassy repression pushed him to leave on the tour; he told his wife he would try to bring her later.

segments.title: Walking out of the Madrid airport
segments.summary: At Madrid he claimed to forget his saxophone, took the street door instead of the plane, and a taxi to a friend's daughter whom he identified with a jewel.

segments.title: Six months in Spain and the government's reaction
segments.summary: He waited six months for papers, wrote for the Finnish radio orchestra and played a Madrid jazz club; Cuban officials took his wife's car and warned her never to leave, and the marriage fell apart.

segments.title: Second day of the interview resumes
segments.summary: The interview resumes the next day, Saturday June 12, 2010, and Jenkins asks him to retell the defection.

segments.title: The defection retold: the saxophone, Chucho and the police
segments.summary: He retells leaving the gate area, Chucho unaware, the wrong door, the jewel, and getting a temporary Spanish visa through the friend's daughter.

segments.title: How Cuban officials and bandmates reacted to his disappearance
segments.summary: Chaos broke out on the plane; Carlos Emilio later said officials were told he stayed to teach, and Enrique Pla said everyone knew he would eventually leave.

segments.title: His mother arrives and the US consul interviews him
segments.summary: His mother came within days and the American consul, wary of his Angola and Soviet travel, finally authorized the green card with a six-month wait.

segments.title: Working and writing in Madrid for six months
segments.summary: His mother sent money, he played with South American musicians at Dahlia's jazz club, wrote arrangements for the Finnish big band and prepared his future quintet.

segments.title: Phoning Cuba with vinegar and salt
segments.summary: He called his family by tricking Madrid payphones with vinegar and salt, a Cuban and Vietnamese trick.

segments.title: His Cuban marriage and the CIA story in Cuba
segments.summary: Pressure on his wife dissolved the marriage, though he refused to sign a divorce, and Cuban media said the CIA paid him two million dollars.

segments.title: Arriving in New York, October 1980: CBS, Dizzy and Amram
segments.summary: He arrived at Kennedy on October 23, 1980, contacted Lundvall at CBS, and got first gigs from Dizzy and David Amram.

segments.title: Arrangements for Kim Records and Chico O'Farrill's jingles
segments.summary: He arranged Spanish-language pop for Kim Records and played jingle sessions with Chico O'Farrill, including a one-note Coca-Cola session with Faddis, Getz and others, and one with Pepper Adams.

segments.title: The Cuban-American community and where he lived
segments.summary: The Cuban community in Union City was not helpful to a jazz career; he lived with his mother, then West New York, then Manhattan Plaza with soprano Brenda Feliciano.

segments.title: Toots Thielemans's illness and the 1981 Dizzy European tour
segments.summary: When Toots Thielemans fell ill, Dizzy asked Paquito by phone to be his guest artist on a five-week European tour in November 1981.

segments.title: Planning the first CBS record and pressure to do pop
segments.summary: Producers wanted a commercial jazz-rock record, with manager Helen Keane, while he wanted a jazz record; he lists the quintet and Eddie Gomez.

segments.title: Soundscape and the Peter Watrous review
segments.summary: His quintet debuted at Verna Gillis's loft Soundscape; Watrous's New York Times review led Lundvall to have him record with that group.

segments.title: Recording Paquito Blowing in two days
segments.summary: The album took two days with the band's club repertoire including Green Dolphin Street and a Monk tribute, and he began writing more.

segments.title: Adding Claudio Roditi to the quintet
segments.summary: Through a Brazilian guitarist in the building, he met Roditi and added him as second horn instead of the percussionist.

segments.title: What the record did for gigs: Vanguard, festivals, Europe
segments.summary: The CBS record broke the gig-and-record catch-22, leading to the Village Vanguard, Blue Note, Chicago and Boston, and Helen Keane's European tours and festivals.

segments.title: First reunion with Irakere members in Europe
segments.summary: At the North Sea Festival only Carlos Emilio dared approach him, and relations later smoothed over.

segments.title: Cuban control of musicians and why Chucho stayed
segments.summary: Defections continued, such as Arturo Sandoval's; he says Chucho promised his mother not to leave and accepted conditions, which Paquito could not do.

segments.title: Live at Keystone Corner, the second CBS album
segments.summary: Helen Keane arranged a live recording at Todd Barkan's San Francisco club, with Roditi on valve trombone.

segments.title: Why he loves the valve trombone
segments.summary: He likes the valve trombone's trombone quality with trumpet-like fingering, and notes Brookmeyer and Raul de Souza, while slide players call it cheating.

segments.title: Claudio Roditi and the Brazilian influence on his writing
segments.summary: Roditi's Brazilian knowledge changed how he composed and led him to work with many Brazilians.

segments.title: Keystone band personnel and Carlos Franzetti's concerto
segments.summary: The band included Ponce, Steve Bailey and pianist Carlos Franzetti, who contributed tunes and wrote him the Jimmy and I clarinet concerto.

segments.title: Writing more: the Aspen woodwind quintet commission
segments.summary: His writing grew, especially after a commission from the Aspen Wind Quintet for Isles Tropicales, leading to more chamber music.

segments.title: Mario Bauza on who plays true Latin jazz
segments.summary: He explains using Latin American elements in jazz, and Bauza's remark that he was the only one doing Latin jazz while others did Afro-Cuban jazz.

segments.title: Latin jazz versus jazz Latin and respecting the sources
segments.summary: Discussing Ray Barretto's distinction, he stresses equal parts and learning a style before mixing it, saying many artists do so irresponsibly.

segments.title: Venezuelan waltzes and learning many Latin American styles
segments.summary: Hearing Venezuelan waltzes from guitarist Farid Haque led him to transcribe and record them and to study the music of Argentina and Uruguay, valuing the differences between styles.

segments.title: Dizzy's United Nations Orchestra begins in 1988
segments.summary: Charlie Fishman shaped the orchestra around Dizzy in 1988; its idea was that the world is one nation of neighbors, matching Paquito's philosophy.

segments.title: Learn the local language: respecting styles instead of imposing bebop
segments.summary: He argues musicians should learn a few words of each musical language rather than impose bebop, like bringing your own ketchup to black beans and rice.

segments.title: Leading the United Nations Orchestra after Dizzy
segments.summary: He and Slide Hampton were musical directors in Dizzy's lifetime and he conducted after Dizzy died, recording A Night in Englewood.

segments.title: Return to clarinet, classical commissions and Webern
segments.summary: Encouraged by Mario Bauza and Dizzy he restarted the clarinet, played Webern with the Brooklyn Philharmonic, quit smoking, and began composing chamber music with popular and Latin elements.

segments.title: Mixing quintet and symphony orchestras: conductors and drummers
segments.summary: Working with orchestras requires concessions; conductors must not wave at the drummer, and Jenkins notes the Cleveland Orchestra saying its players do not swing.

segments.title: Writing for orchestra according to each instrument's limits
segments.summary: He says write for what strings and horns can do, let the quintet swing and the strings play the mellow part, and treat the orchestra as a beautiful instrument you cannot force.

segments.title: Preparing himself: lifelong symphony experience and feeling the beat
segments.summary: Having worked with symphonies since childhood, he understands their weight, and contrasts that with a Black Cuban sense of rhythm.

segments.title: Rhythm across cultures and the will to learn
segments.summary: Vienna waltzes, Venezuelan merengue and tango show different senses of rhythm; Wynton Marsalis told him you learn only if you want to, and a violinist who played Bach claimed to be unfamiliar with Cachao.

segments.title: Chamber ensembles: Imani Winds and Yo-Yo Ma
segments.summary: He praises Imani Winds and writing for Yo-Yo Ma and notes the difficulty of syncopation for classical players.

segments.title: Jazz and classical education ignoring each other
segments.summary: Classical and jazz schools alienate each other, illustrated by a youth symphony trombonist frightened by a simple montuno figure; his father never taught jazz but took him to those who could.

segments.title: His father's open mind toward improvisers
segments.summary: Although a classical player, his father valued improvisers, in contrast to the tradition that is only slowly changing.

segments.title: Young musicians crossing worlds and a general music education
segments.summary: More young players move between jazz and classical; he would teach both groups together, giving everyone a general music grounding as Gunther Schuller proposed.

segments.title: Festival advisor roles and whether jazz is dying
segments.summary: He explains his advisory ties to the D.C. Jazz Festival and the Uruguay festival, and rejects claims that jazz ended with its giants, as Chick Corea also said.

segments.title: Jazz as a roach, and jazz born from nothing
segments.summary: Jenkins quotes Jackie McLean that jazz cannot be killed; Paquito says jazz was made from scarce means, like the banjo and drum set.

segments.title: What being an NEA Jazz Master means to him
segments.summary: He takes the honor humbly, as a responsibility among distinguished peers, and rarely uses the title.
